Forest
for'est
n. (an extensive wood; rendering Hebrew yaar)
From the Latin foris, out of doors, through the Low Latin foresta — originally land outside the enclosed and cultivated ground. Hebrew yaar is a wood or thicket, and in the prophets it regularly stands for what is dense, wild, and ripe for the axe.

Biblical Definition

Forest in Scripture is chiefly the prophets' image for proud height brought down, and secondarily a statement of God's ownership of the wild. Isaiah closes his oracle against Assyria with an axe laid to timber: “he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one” (Isaiah 10:34) — the cedars of Lebanon being the ancient world's emblem of unassailable stature, so that felling them is a figure of empires cut off. Micah turns the same image against Jerusalem itself and it is the more shocking for it: “Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest” (Micah 3:12) — the temple mount reverting to scrub, a prophecy the elders of Judah still remembered a century later in Jeremiah's trial. The Psalter uses the forest differently, to settle a question about sacrifice: God tells Israel he has no need of their bulls, “for every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills” (Psalm 50:10). Worship is not provisioning. The wild belongs to God already, and he asks for thanksgiving instead.

Webster 1828 Definition

An extensive wood, originally land outside cultivation. In the prophets the forest is proud height awaiting the axe; in Psalm 50 it is proof that God needs nothing men could bring him.

expand to see more

FOREST, n. [Low L. foresta, from L. foris, out of doors.] An extensive wood, or a large tract of land covered with trees.

2. In law, a tract of ground kept for game and under particular regulations.

3. Figuratively, whatever is dense, wild, or uncultivated.

4. In Scripture, an emblem of proud height cut down; as, he shall cut down the thickets of the forest, Isa. 10.

5. Of God's ownership of the wild; as, every beast of the forest is mine, Psa. 50.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 10:34 — "And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one."

Micah 3:12 — "Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest."

Psalm 50:10 — "For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills."

Genesis 1:10 — "And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good."

Modern Corruption

Worship is easily treated as provision for God — our giving, our effort, our contribution to his cause. Psalm 50 answers that every beast of the forest is already his, and asks for thanksgiving instead.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The distortion is devotional rather than lexical, and Psalm 50 addresses it directly. God tells a sacrificing people that if he were hungry he would not tell them, since the world is his and the fulness thereof. The temptation is perennial: to imagine that God is somehow supplied by our offerings, and thereby to think of giving as a transaction that puts him under obligation. Every prosperity scheme rests on that error, and so, more quietly, does a great deal of respectable religion.

The principle to recover joins the two images. God owns the forest, so nothing we bring adds to him; and God fells forests, so no height we build is beyond his axe. Micah 3:12 is the sharpest form of the second point, since it aims at the temple itself — the place Judah trusted as a guarantee, which God said he would leave as wooded high ground. What he asks instead is stated in the same Psalm: offer unto God thanksgiving, and pay thy vows unto the most High.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yaar is a forest, wood, or thicket, and by extension a honeycomb dripping in the wood. Choresh is a wooded height, and erez is the cedar, the forest tree of Lebanon.

expand to see more

Hebrew yaar (H3293) — forest, wood, thicket; the prophets' emblem of dense proud growth.

Hebrew choresh (H2793) — a wood, a wooded height; where David hid in the wilderness of Ziph.

Hebrew erez (H730) — cedar; the cedars of Lebanon, the tallest timber known to Israel.

Hebrew levanon (H3844) — Lebanon; its forest stands for imperial stature in Isaiah 10.

Greek hule (G5208) — wood, a forest; how great a matter a little fire kindleth, James 3:5.

Usage

"Of empires felled: he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron (Isaiah 10:34)."

"Of the temple mount reverting to scrub: the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest (Micah 3:12)."

"Of God's prior ownership of all we might offer: every beast of the forest is mine (Psalm 50:10)."
